summary.text: A 35-year-old man with a longstanding history of developmental delay, limited schooling, poor social functioning and lifelong dependence on family had multiple hospitalizations over the last 2 years under a working diagnosis of schizophrenia and received antipsychotics including risperidone, olanzapine and clozapine, with aggression and poor treatment response.

He was brought to the emergency department with mutism, immobility and refusal to eat; on admission he was mute and immobile with negativism and posturing consistent with catatonia. He lacked the ability to communicate, was unresponsive and poorly groomed, and the physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Neuroimaging, liver and renal function, blood tests and EEG were reported normal. The authors attribute the catatonia to protracted antipsychotic exposure.

A lorazepam challenge partly alleviated catatonia and antipsychotics were discontinued. Re-evaluation with developmental history and neuropsychological testing confirmed moderate intellectual disability with behavioral disturbance rather than primary psychotic disorder. Management was revised to supportive interventions, family psychoeducation and behavioral strategies, and the family was instructed on caregiving.

At the 3-month follow-up he had reduced aggression, enhanced mobility and increased interaction, catatonic symptoms had not recurred, and the family reported improved functioning and reduced caregiver burden despite persistent intellectual disability; the family reported relief at the precise diagnosis.
